prohibited_recommendations: Do not give benzodiazepines or other sedatives for agitation or sleep: they precipitate and prolong hepatic encephalopathy; manage agitation with reorientation, a safe environment and treatment of the precipitant (EASL 2022).
Do not prescribe sedating opioids, which precipitate and prolong HE; for pain use acetaminophen up to 2 g per day.
Do not dismiss subtle cognitive complaints in cirrhosis because the ammonia is normal or the Child-Pugh class is A.
Do not start a cholinesterase inhibitor for presumed Alzheimer disease: the profile is covert HE with reversible contributors.
required_recommendations: Treat covert HE that is affecting his work: lactulose titrated to 2-3 soft bowel movements per day (ACG 2026 recommendation 10; EASL 2022), avoiding over-titration, which causes dehydration, hypokalemia and kidney injury; review symptoms, adherence and psychometric performance at 4-8 weeks.
Restore CPAP adherence with sleep medicine (mask refit, auto-titrating device), aiming for at least 4 hours per night.
Review the indication for long-term omeprazole and deprescribe it (on-demand use or an H2 receptor antagonist) if none remains; PPI use is associated with HE in cirrhosis.
Counsel him on driving: covert HE impairs driving and raises crash risk; advise against driving until reassessed after treatment, and document the advice.

avoided_actions.rationale: No clinical suspicion for hepatopulmonary syndrome, portopulmonary hypertension, or endocarditis; echocardiography is not part of the HE workup.
Amyloid PET has no role in HE workup; reversible metabolic encephalopathy is the issue, not Alzheimer pathology.
DaTscan has no role in HE workup; the question is metabolic encephalopathy, not nigrostriatal degeneration.
FDG PET has no role in HE workup; metabolic encephalopathy is reversible with precipitant control and does not require nuclear functional imaging.

accepted: Covert hepatic encephalopathy (PHES -5) in well-compensated NASH cirrhosis (Child-Pugh A, MELD-Na 7), with untreated obstructive sleep apnea (CPAP non-adherence, nocturnal hypoxemia) and long-term PPI use as contributors; ammonia within the reference range (48 µmol/L); no asterixis.

differential.diagnosis: Obstructive sleep apnea cognitive decline (untreated CPAP)
differential.key_features: CPAP use 3.2 hours per night with SpO2 below 90% for 18% of the night causes daytime sleepiness and cognitive slowing and adds to covert HE; treat both.
A 6-week course with sleep inversion and psychomotor slowing on PHES fits covert HE; reassess cognition after HE and OSA are treated.
No sedatives; omeprazole, metformin and amlodipine do not explain the picture.
No low mood reported; screen (for example PHQ-9) if symptoms persist after treatment.

key_clinical_evidence: HE is a clinical diagnosis: West Haven grade, evidence of liver disease and exclusion of other causes of altered mental status (ACG 2026; EASL 2022).

An elevated ammonia neither grades nor confirms hepatic encephalopathy and repeat levels are not used to guide treatment; a normal ammonia in a confused patient with cirrhosis should prompt a search for another cause (ACG 2026 recommendation 5 and key concept 14; EASL 2022).
Child-Pugh A (5: bilirubin 0.8 1, albumin 3.8 1, INR 1.1 1, no ascites 1, no clinically evident encephalopathy 1); MELD-Na 7 (creatinine 0.9, bilirubin 0.8, INR 1.1, sodium 140).

Covert HE is minimal HE or West Haven grade 1; overt HE is grade 2 or higher (ACG 2026 key concept 1). Covert HE is diagnosed by psychometric tests such as PHES once other causes are excluded (EASL 2022).

Covert HE affects about a third to a half of patients with cirrhosis; it impairs quality of life and driving and predicts overt HE, and treatment can be offered when it affects daily life (EASL 2022).
PPIs have been associated with HE risk via gut dysbiosis; deprescribe when not indicated.
Driving safety is impaired in covert HE — counsel and document.

patient.history_present_illness: Mr. A. is a 58-year-old accountant with well-compensated NASH cirrhosis, obstructive sleep apnea on CPAP, and type 2 diabetes, presenting at his wife's insistence for cognitive evaluation. She noticed 6 weeks of progressive forgetfulness, difficulty with sequential tasks at work (he made errors in spreadsheets he normally manages perfectly), increased irritability, and a reversal of sleep pattern (day drowsiness, nighttime wakefulness). He denies confusion. He has no jaundice, no ascites, no asterixis. His wife reports he frequently removes the CPAP mask overnight; the download from his sleep clinic last week showed average use of 3.2 hours per night, with SpO2 below 90% for 18% of the night. He has taken omeprazole for 5 years and also takes metformin.
